# Shared language rules

[Glyph index](glyphs.qmd)

## Reading expressions

Five rules decide how code reads. [Language principles](principles.qmd) explains why the notation works this way.

1. **Brackets and parentheses.** A [bracket list](glyphs/brackets.qmd) such as `[a b c]` is a vector. `[x]` is a one-item vector. A strand of literals can leave the brackets out: `1 2 3` is one vector. Parentheses group, whatever they hold. With `⋄`, parentheses are used to write a vector of rows: `(4 ⋄ 4 5)` is `[[4] [4 5]]`.
2. **Runs.** A *run* is a sequence of tokens with no spaces between them. A bracketed, parenthesised or braced group counts as one token. Each run is evaluated first, and then the runs combine. Parentheses round an expression group it.
3. **Application.** Right to left, with no precedence between functions. A function takes everything to its right as its right argument, and the subject directly to its left as its left argument. An operator takes the function to its left and one item to its right. A run that ends in a dyadic operator takes the next run as that item. Subjects side by side form a strand: `a b` is `[a b]`.
4. **Trains.** A run that ends in a function is a *train*, a function built from the right.
5. **Assignment.** `←` assigns everything after it to the run before it.

```bpl
2×3+4                ⍝ 14
2×3 + 4              ⍝ 10
(2×3)+4              ⍝ 10
10-3-2               ⍝ 9
```

### Terms

Every [value](#term-value) is an [atom](#term-atom) or an [array](#term-array): atoms are [numbers](#term-number), [characters](#term-character) and [functions](#term-function), [scalars](#term-scalar) are arrays of [rank](#term-rank) 0, [units](#term-unit) are atoms and scalars, and [subjects](#term-subject) are all values except functions.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [value]{#term-value} | a number, character, function or array |
| [atom]{#term-atom} | a value that isn't an array: a number, character or function |
| [number]{#term-number} | an approximate real or complex number, or an exact integer or rational, as [Numbers](#numbers) describes |
| [character]{#term-character} | one Unicode character, written in single quotes: `'a'` |
| [function]{#term-function} | a primitive, dfn, train or derived function, which applies to arguments |
| [pervasive function]{#term-pervasive-function} | a function that applies to each atom of its arguments, through any nesting: `1+[2 ⊂3]` is `[3 ⊂4]` |
| [array]{#term-array} | a rectangular collection of values along zero or more axes |
| [rank]{#term-rank} | the number of axes: a vector has rank 1, and atoms and scalars have rank 0 |
| [scalar]{#term-scalar} | an array of rank 0, holding one value: `⊂5` is a scalar holding the number 5, and `5` is a number |
| [unit]{#term-unit} | a rank-0 value: a number, character, function or scalar |
| [subject]{#term-subject} | a value that isn't a function: a number, character or array |
| [cell]{#term-cell} | a sub-array made of an array's last k axes, called a k-cell: a matrix's rows are its 1-cells. A 0-cell is the unit at one position, the atom there or the array there enclosed. When k is at least the array's rank, the whole array is its one cell |
| [frame]{#term-frame} | the axes before the cells, with one cell at each position |
| [assembly]{#term-assembly} | building one array from results, one for each position of a frame: the shape is the frame followed by the results' shape, each result fills its position with its items, and shorter results are padded with fill |
| [literal]{#term-literal} | a number, character, string, `∞`, `⍬`, or a constant: `$t` true, `$f` false or `$n` NaN |
| [strand]{#term-strand} | subjects side by side, read as a vector without brackets: `1 2 3` is `[1 2 3]`, and `a b` is `[a b]` |
| [run]{#term-run} | a sequence of tokens with no spaces between them |
| [argument]{#term-argument} | a subject a function applies to |
| [operand]{#term-operand} | a value an operator applies to |
| [expression]{#term-expression} | a run, group or statement that ends in a subject |
| [train]{#term-train} | a run, group or statement that ends in a function |
| [fork]{#term-fork} | three parts of a train, `f g h`, giving `(f ⍵) g (h ⍵)`, or `A g h` with a subject on the left, giving `A g (h ⍵)` |
| [atop]{#term-atop} | two parts of a train, `f g`, giving `f (g ⍵)` |
| [bind]{#term-bind} | a subject directly before a function in a train, fixing its left argument: `2×` is `2⍃×` |

### Strands

Numbers in every form, `∞`, `¯∞`, `⍬`, characters, strings and the constants `$t`, `$f` and `$n` are literals. A constant is `$` and one letter. Literals separated by spaces form a *strand*, which is one vector. Names never join a strand, including system constants such as `•a`. The parser forms strands before it forms runs. Inside brackets without `;`, every space separates items instead of forming a strand.

### Brackets and parentheses

[Brackets](glyphs/brackets.qmd) always write a vector, whatever the number of items: `[5]` is a one-item vector. `;` separates items that contain spaces. `⋄` stacks rows into an array of higher rank. Each row is a major cell. A row of one number has rank 0. For example, `[1 ⋄ 2]` is the vector `1 2`. Write a column as `[[1] ⋄ [2]]`.

[Parentheses](glyphs/parentheses.qmd) group, whatever they hold: `(1 2)` is `1 2`, `(x)` is `x`, and `(-)` is `-`. `⊂` encloses a subject: `⊂[1 2]` is a scalar holding a vector. [`fᵘ`](scripts.qmd#superscripts) is a scalar holding the function `f`.

With `⋄`, parentheses are used to write a vector of rows instead. Each row is a bracket list, even a row with one item. For example, `(4 ⋄ 4 5 ⋄ 4 5 6)` is `[[4] [4 5] [4 5 6]]`. With a trailing `⋄`, the result is a one-item vector holding one row: `(1 2 ⋄)` is `[[1 2]]`. Rows in brackets form a flat array, and rows in parentheses form a nested vector.

```bpl
⍴[5]                 ⍝ [1]ₓ
⍴[[1] ⋄ [2]]         ⍝ [2 1]ₓ
(1 2)≡[1 2]          ⍝ $t
(4 ⋄ 4 5)≡[[4] [4 5]]  ⍝ $t
(1+2)×3              ⍝ 9
```

```bpl
+/1 2 3              ⍝ 6
≢"ab" "cd"           ⍝ 2ₓ
a←1 ⋄ b←2 ⋄ [a b]    ⍝ 1 2
```

### Runs

Spaces separate runs outside brackets. A line break inside parentheses or brackets counts as a space. Inside braces, a line break separates statements. Each run must reduce to one value: a subject, a function, or a lone operator such as the `/` in `+ / x`. Otherwise it is a `SYNTAX` error.

```bpl
a←1 ⋄ b←2 ⋄ c←3 ⋄ d←4 ⋄ a+b × c+d   ⍝ 21
x←3 ⋄ x+1 ÷ 2                        ⍝ 2
+ / 1 2 3                            ⍝ 6
```

### Operators and operands

Operators bind before function application. An operator's left operand is the whole function to its left. Its right operand is the one item to its right. That item ends at the next space. A strand of literals counts as one item. For example, `f⍤1 M` applies `f` at rank 1 to `M`, and `f⍤1 2 M` has rank `1 2`. Put a vector argument after a literal operand in brackets, as in `f⍤1[2 3]`, and a single number in parentheses, as in `f⍣¯2(5)`. A run that ends in a dyadic operator takes the next run as its right operand, as if no space came between them. For example, `f⍤ 1 M` is `f⍤1 M`, and in `⌊⌾ 10× x` the operand of `⌾` is the whole of `10×`.

```bpl
m←2 3⍴⍳6 ⋄ +/⍤1 m               ⍝ 3 12
m←2 3⍴⍳6 ⋄ +/⍤ 1 m              ⍝ 3 12
x←5 ⋄ 1+⍣3 x                     ⍝ 8
1+⍣3(5)                          ⍝ 8
```

Where an operator takes a function, an array operand acts as a constant function, as `A⍨` does. Reduce and scan still need a function, and `5/` is an error. Replicate is `#`.

```bpl
5¨ 1 2 3                         ⍝ 5 5 5
```

Names hold subjects, functions or operators, resolved at execution time. Arrays contain numbers, characters, functions and arrays.

A name consists of letters, `∆` and `⍙`. A digit ends a name, as it ends a glyph. For example, `f2` is `f` applied to 2, the same way `⍳2` is `⍳` applied to 2. `_` adds the next character to the name, whatever it is. For example, `x_1` and `x_+` are names. After `_`, a run of digits stays in the name, as in `x_12`. Apart from the lone name `_`, a name can't end in `_`. A lone `_` followed by a space, `]`, `)`, `←`, `;`, `⋄` or the end of the line is the name `_`. Assign to `_` a value nothing reads, as in `[k _ v]←⍵`. After a dot, digits stay in the key: `T.q1` is the entry with key `q1`.

```bpl
x_1←10 ⋄ x_12←20 ⋄ x_1+x_12   ⍝ 30
f←- ⋄ f2                       ⍝ ¯2
T←["q1":5] ⋄ T.q1             ⍝ 5
[k _ v]←1 2 3 ⋄ k+v            ⍝ 4
```

### Subjects side by side

Subjects side by side form a strand. `a b` is the vector `[a b]`, with one item for each subject. Each run is evaluated before the strand forms. `a b+1` is therefore `[a (b+1)]`. A strand of literals counts as one item: `x 1 2` is `[x [1 2]]`.

```bpl
a←1 2 ⋄ b←3 4 ⋄ a b        ⍝ [[1 2] [3 4]]
a←1 ⋄ b←2 ⋄ a b+1          ⍝ 1 3
x←5 ⋄ x 1 2                ⍝ [5 [1 2]]
```

[Index](glyphs/squad.qmd) `⌷` selects along the leading axis. The result has the shape of the positions, followed by the shape of each selected cell.

```bpl
v←10 20 30 40 ⋄ [[2 0]]⌷v       ⍝ 30 10
v←10 20 30 40 ⋄ ¯1⌷v            ⍝ 40
v←10 20 30 40 ⋄ [⊂1]⌷v          ⍝ ⊂20
v←10 20 30 40 ⋄ [[1]]⌷v         ⍝ [20]
```

A [subscript](scripts.qmd#subscripts) selects one position on the leading axis: `v₁` is `1⌷v`, and `v₋₁` is `¯1⌷v`.

### Trains

BPL builds a train from its last function leftwards, as APL does. A function and the item before it form a *fork* with the part already built: `f g h` gives `(f ⍵) g (h ⍵)`. When that item is a subject, `A g h` gives `A g (h ⍵)`. A subject directly before the part already built *binds* to it. For example, `2×` is `2⍃×`. A function left over at the start makes an *atop*: `f g` gives `f (g ⍵)`.

```bpl
f←32+1.8× ⋄ f100     ⍝ 212
(+/÷≢) 1 2 3 6       ⍝ 3
(0.5×⊢+÷) 2          ⍝ 1.25
2 (1-×) 5            ⍝ ¯9
```

With two arguments, a fork `f g h` gives `(⍺ f ⍵) g (⍺ h ⍵)`. With a subject on the left, `A g h` gives `A g (⍺ h ⍵)`. An atop `f g` gives `f (⍺ g ⍵)`. A bound function is monadic: `3 (2×) 4` is a `SYNTAX` error.

The reading depends on whether a space comes before the argument. `+/÷≢ x` is the mean of `x`, and `+/÷≢x` is `+/(÷(≢x))`. Where a train's subjects and functions alternate, as in `32+1.8×`, both readings give the same result. A name followed by a name needs a space. A literal can touch a name, as it touches a glyph: `1+⌽f5`. A name as the argument, inside a longer expression, goes in parentheses: `1+⌽f(x)`. A run that starts with a function is a call: `×2` is the sign of 2.

### Assignment

The target of `←` is the run before it: a name, a selection such as `(1⌷v)`, `v₁`, `v.[1]` or `T.x`, a list of names such as `[a b]`, or one of these followed by a function for [modified assignment](glyphs/assign.qmd). A named function joins the target in parentheses, because a space would end the run: `a(f)←3` is `a←a f 3`, at top level and in dfns. The value is everything to the right of `←`, up to the end of the statement or group. `a←1 b←2` is not two assignments, because the first `←` takes `1 b←2` as its value. Independent assignments need `⋄`.

```bpl
v←10 20 30 ⋄ v₁←7 ⋄ v            ⍝ 10 7 30
[a b]←3 4 ⋄ a×b                  ⍝ 12
a←1 ⋄ f←+ ⋄ a(f)←3 ⋄ a           ⍝ 4
```

### Precedence

From tightest to loosest:

1. within a run, right to left
2. across runs, right to left
3. the pipe `→`, whose stages run left to right
4. assignment `←`
5. the error guard `::`
6. `⋄`, which separates statements, and `?`, which ends a predicate
7. `;`, which separates a dfn's bodies

Spaces change grouping only at the first two levels.

`→` separates pipeline stages. Each function receives the previous result as its right argument. `←` takes the whole pipeline as its value.

```bpl
total←1+2×3 → 2× ⋄ total   ⍝ 14
```

### Mixed spacing

- `x ×2` is a strand of `x` and the sign of 2, with no error.
- `10 -/1 2 3` is a strand of `10` and the reduction: `10 2`. A seeded reduction needs the same spacing on both sides of the function: `10-/1 2 3`.
- `x[2]+ 1` is a `SYNTAX` error. The run `x[2]+` is a train in which `[2]` and `x` both bind to `+`. The sum of item 2 and 1 is `(2⌷x)+1`.

## Numbers

[Numbers](numbers.qmd) covers how numbers are written, exact and approximate arithmetic, storage, infinities, NaN and Booleans.

## Arrays, nesting and fill

[Arrays](arrays.qmd) covers atoms and arrays, shape and rank, nesting, fill, keys and functions held in arrays.

## Agreement and pervasion

Pervasive functions align leading axes. Missing trailing dimensions count as 1. Equal dimensions agree. A dimension of length 1 expands, including to zero. Axes of length 1 remain. Other mismatches: `LENGTH`.

```bpl
[1 2 3 ⋄ 4 5 6]+10 20 ⍝ [11 12 13 ⋄ 24 25 26]
[[10] ⋄ [20]]+[1 2 3 ⋄] ⍝ [11 12 13 ⋄ 21 22 23]
⍴[[10] ⋄]+1 2 3       ⍝ [3 1]ₓ
```

Pervasion repeats these rules inside nested items. Each and rank frames also use leading agreement. Products, replication, indexing and assignment have their own rules.

This extends APL agreement. NumPy aligns trailing axes.

## Axes and indices

Positions and axes count from 0. Negative positions and axes count from the end. A count or position must be an integer, or a float within comparison tolerance of one. [Index](glyphs/squad.qmd) `⌷` selects along leading axes: `1⌷m` is row 1, the second row. `∞` selects a whole axis. After an array, [dot indexing](glyphs/dot.qmd) writes the same selection: `m.[∞ 1]` is `∞ 1⌷m`.

[Axis](glyphs/axis.qmd) `⍠` applies a function along axes given as numbers or names, as in `+/⍠0` and `+/⍠"month"`. [Rank](glyphs/rank.qmd) `⍤` applies it to trailing cells. `⍤0` passes an atom item as itself, and an array item as a scalar holding it. `/ \ ⌽ ,` default to the last axis, and `⌿ ⍀ ⊖ ⍪` to the first. Replicate `N#Y` and the partitions `N⊂Y` and `N⊆Y` work along the first axis. Encode `⊤` puts its digits on the last axis, and Decode `⊥` reads them from it. Structural functions also accept axis lists.

```bpl
m←[1 2 3 ⋄ 4 5 6]
1⌷m                  ⍝ 4 5 6
∞ 1⌷m                ⍝ 2 5
+/⍠0 m               ⍝ 5 7 9
```

## Equality and ordering

Exact/exact comparison is exact. Approximate comparison uses relative tolerance `1E¯14`. Infinity equals itself, never a finite number.

```bpl
0.3=0.1+0.2          ⍝ $t
1r3=1x÷3x            ⍝ $t
```

Search functions compare major cells. `⍳` and `⍸` search their left argument, and `∊ ~ ∩` search their right. The other argument's cells have the same rank as the searched argument's major cells. The searched argument can't be a unit, because a unit has no major cells. For example, `s~" "` removes spaces, but `s~' '` is a `RANK` error.

Search, membership, match and grouping use tolerant comparison. Because tolerance isn't transitive, search and grouping compare against the first matching representative.

Grade and interval index ignore tolerance. Numbers come before characters, and characters before nested arrays. Numbers compare by value, and complex numbers by real part, then imaginary part. Characters compare by code point. Nested arrays compare rank, then ravel lexicographically, then shape, ignoring prototypes. Grade is stable. Pervasive ordering (`< ≤ > ≥ ⌊ ⌈`) requires reals.

## Functions and effects

Dfns use lexical scope. Plain assignment is local. Modified and selective updates target the nearest binding. Arrays have value semantics: updating one name leaves other copies unchanged.

```bpl
a←1 2 ⋄ b←a ⋄ a₀←9 ⋄ b ⍝ 1 2
```

Every statement in a dfn body runs, and the body's last statement gives the result. A final assignment returns its value silently. Top-level assignments also retain their value without display. See [Dfns](dfns.qmd).

Evaluation is right-to-left, including fork arms. Items inside brackets evaluate left-to-right, as statements do.

Empty Each, rank, Outer and Inner product call the operand on prototypes. Empty scan makes no calls. Generic reduction associates right; float sum/product may reassociate. All scans accumulate left-to-right.

## Errors

| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `DOMAIN` | Invalid values or unknown inverse |
| `RANK` / `LENGTH` | Invalid rank or shape/count agreement |
| `INDEX` | Invalid position |
| `SYNTAX` | Invalid syntax or call form |
| `VALUE` | Undefined name or missing value |

Every error shows its source location. Unsupported features and resource limits have separate errors.
